teaser: At 55, broke and out of fashion, Rembrandt dressed up as a saint and kept his own tired face.
review_notes:
Cindy Sherman's History Portraits series dated 1988 to 1990.
Claim that this is the only self-portrait in which Rembrandt takes the role of a named biblical figure as the single subject (he appears as a bystander or as the prodigal son in earlier narrative pictures).
Count of roughly 80 self-portraits across paintings, etchings and drawings.
Size 91 x 77 cm.
The sword hilt is very dark in the image; find block may be hard, please test.
1660 arrangement in which Hendrickje and Titus formally employed Rembrandt.

lesson.text: Between 1988 and 1990 the American photographer Cindy Sherman made a series called History Portraits. She photographed herself in costume as figures from old paintings: madonnas, noblemen, monks. Critics called it a new way of asking who a self-portrait really shows. Rembrandt had asked the same thing in 1661, with a turban, a sword and a sheaf of paper.

He was 55. Five years earlier he had gone bankrupt, and his house and art collection had been sold. In 1660 his partner Hendrickje and his son Titus set up an art business and made him their employee, a legal arrangement that kept his creditors away from his new work.

Around 1661 he painted a group of apostles, the first followers of Christ, as half-length figures. They are worn, ordinary men, each alone with his thoughts. For one of them, Paul, he used the model he knew best.

Rembrandt made about 80 self-portraits in paint, ink and print over forty years, more than almost any artist before him. This is the only one in which he is the single subject and plays a named figure from the Bible.

lesson.title: A face, not a mask
lesson.text: Nothing here flatters. Start at the top of the head and work down.

spots.title: The turban
spots.text: A white cloth wound around the head, painted in thick ridges of paint that catch real light. It suggests the Eastern world of the Bible. It also sits where a halo would.

spots.title: The forehead
spots.text: The eyebrows go up and the brow folds into deep creases. It is the look of someone caught in a thought, or shrugging: well, here I am.

spots.title: Eyes and nose
spots.text: One eye sinks into shadow. The nose is broad and reddish, the skin slack. He had painted this face for decades and spares it nothing.

lesson.text: So how do we know this is Paul and not simply Rembrandt in a headscarf? Painters used attributes, objects that work like name tags for saints. Paul has two. Both are in the picture, and Rembrandt has hidden both in the dark.

The first is easy: the bundle of pages glowing at the lower right. Paul wrote the Epistles, the letters to the first Christian communities that fill a large part of the New Testament. The second attribute takes more patience.
Paul's other attribute is a sword. Only its handle shows, poking out of his cloak. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The hilt
spots.text: A dull glint below the chest: the grip of a sword tucked under the coat. Tradition says Paul was beheaded with one, and he wrote of the word of God as “the sword of the Spirit.”

lesson.text: A sword you can barely see and letters you cannot read. Rembrandt gives the saint's badges as little light as possible and spends it on the forehead instead. The holy man matters less to him than the aging one.

Why Paul? Before his conversion Paul hunted down Christians. He later called himself the worst of sinners, saved by grace alone. That idea sat at the heart of the Protestant faith Rembrandt grew up in. A man with debts and a public disgrace behind him might well have felt at home in the role.
The painting is signed and dated at the left edge, level with the shoulder, in thin brown letters that almost melt into the wall: Rembrandt f. 1661. The “f” stands for the Latin fecit, “made it.”
Dressing up did not hide Rembrandt. A borrowed role let him say something about himself that a plain self-portrait could not: I am flawed, and I know it.

The picture is small, 91 by 77 centimeters (about 36 by 30 inches), and hangs in the Rijksmuseum. Sherman vanishes into her costumes, and you are meant to wonder who is under them. With Rembrandt it works the other way: you forget the costume within seconds and are left with the man.

quiz.question: Which two objects identify the figure as Paul?
quiz.explanation: Paul's attributes are the sword and the pages of his letters.

quiz.question: What is an attribute in a painting of a saint?
options: An object that identifies the saint

quiz.question: What had happened to Rembrandt five years before this picture?
options: He had been made court painter
quiz.explanation: His house and collection were sold after his bankruptcy.

quiz.question: Where does Rembrandt put most of the light?
quiz.explanation: The saint's badges stay in the dark; the face gets the light.

facts.text: The sword in the painting is fully drawn and brightly lit.
facts.explanation: Only its handle shows, half hidden under the cloak.

facts.text: Before his conversion, Paul persecuted Christians.
facts.explanation: He later called himself the worst of sinners.

facts.text: Rembrandt painted himself only two or three times in his life.
facts.explanation: He made about 80 self-portraits in paint, ink and print.
